title: Giving well
hook: On Benefits: give freely, promptly, and without reminding (On Benefits 1.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: two cities, the town where you live and the whole human world. Your line was two cities. What did you do for each one? Day five hundred twelve.

Everyone has met this person. They lent you forty dollars in college, and somehow it comes up at every dinner since. Or the relative whose birthday present arrives with a short speech about how hard it was to find. The gift was real. The money was real. And yet something about the way it was given turned it sour, and you'd almost rather have gone without. Seneca noticed the same thing in Rome. So he wrote one of his longest works, seven books of it, about one ordinary act. Today: giving well.
screen: `THE FORTY DOLLARS AT EVERY DINNER.` → `A GIFT GIVEN BADLY.` → `GIVING WELL.`

segments.voice: First, the book. It's called On Benefits, written to a friend named Aebutius Liberalis. The Latin word is beneficium: a good deed, a favor, anything done for someone else's good. Seneca opens by saying that among all the mistakes of careless living, hardly any is worse than this one: we don't know how to give, and we don't know how to receive. Second, freely. A favor done to get something back, he says, isn't a benefit at all. It's an investment. And when people turn out ungrateful, he doesn't tell us to stop. Even after a bad harvest, he says, the farmer sows again. Third, promptly. In book two he says to give without hesitation. A favor dragged out with delays, or one the other person has to beg for, loses most of its sweetness, because asking costs people something. An old Latin proverb, usually credited to the writer Publilius Syrus, puts it shortly: whoever gives quickly gives twice. Fourth, then forget it. Here's the line that becomes our carry. Seneca says there's a law between the two people in a benefit: one should forget at once that he gave, and the other should never forget that he received. Reminding someone of what you did for them, he says, is close to asking for it back. It turns a gift into a bill. Notice how practical this is. Seneca isn't asking for bigger gifts. He's asking for cleaner ones: no strings, no waiting, no speeches afterward. The forty dollars would have been a lovely gift. Only the remembering ruined it.
screen: `ON BENEFITS: SEVEN BOOKS ON ONE ACT.` · `FREELY: THE FARMER SOWS AGAIN.` · `PROMPTLY: DON'T MAKE THEM BEG.` · `THEN FORGET THAT YOU GAVE.` · then, large: `GIVE, THEN FORGET.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you've been meaning to give and keep putting off. A reply someone's waiting for. A book to return. A thank-you note. An hour of help. Some money you said you'd send. Picture giving it today, quickly, without a speech. Picture the other person's face. Then picture walking away and not mentioning it again, ever. Notice which part is harder. The bell holds the time.
Giving well. Seneca's On Benefits: give freely, give promptly, and once it's given, let yourself forget it. Today's word.
Your line: give, then forget. Give one thing today before anyone has to ask twice, and then don't bring it up again. Day five hundred twelve.

howItsDone: People who read Seneca's On Benefits often take up three habits from it: give without expecting a return, give before being asked twice, and never remind the other person of the favor.

fork.setup: a friend asks if you can help them move on Saturday. you can. what fits On Benefits?
options: say yes right away, and show up.
say maybe, and decide Friday night.
help, and remind them of it later.
fork.reveal: give without hesitation, Seneca says: a favor someone has to wait or beg for loses most of its sweetness.

original.note: Latin, from bene 'well' and facere 'to do': a good deed, Seneca's subject in On Benefits.

trapdoor: what it means: how you give matters as much as what: freely, promptly, and then forgotten by you.
what a scholar hears: in Rome favors bound patrons and clients in a web of debts; On Benefits tries to lift giving out of that ledger.

notes: On Benefits is addressed to Aebutius Liberalis and runs to seven books: confirm. Reviewer softened 'the longest essay he ever wrote' to 'one of his longest works', since the Natural Questions and the Letters are longer and the ranking is debatable.

1.1: among the errors of careless living, few are worse than not knowing how to give and receive benefits; the 'sow again after a bad harvest' image (1.1, post malam segetem serendum est): confirm placement.
2.1–2: give without hesitation; a benefit that must be begged for or is delayed loses its value. Paraphrased.
2.10–11: the law between giver and receiver (one should forget at once that he gave, the other never forget that he received); reminding is close to demanding repayment. Confirm section numbers.
The proverb 'bis dat qui cito dat' is popularly credited to Publilius Syrus (his sentence reads 'inopi beneficium bis dat qui dat celeriter'); confirm attribution.
